interactions.summary: Jiang restarts the afternoon session by telling livestream viewers the class schedule, warning that he is offering only one English-language interpretation, and arguing that Dante must ultimately be experienced aloud in Tuscan because the poem is divinely inspired and perfect.
A student reads the next tercet aloud, introducing an image of warm rays stripping snow and leaving the mind bare of error before a new living light appears.
Jiang interprets the passage as Dante's refusal of passive church obedience, saying genuine understanding requires open debate and a teacher must let students make errors.
The student continues reading the line that presents heaven as a body whose power grounds the being of all things.

Jiang pauses on the line about a cosmic body and turns it into a classroom exercise, asking for alternative metaphors for the universe; students answer with images like a big ball, God, and a turtle standing on an elephant.

speaker_notes.note: These are student read-aloud spans from the poem and should stay distinct from Jiang's interpretive claims.
The turtle-elephant cosmology is a student contribution that Jiang paraphrases and folds into his metaphor exercise.

claims.claim: Jiang says the class is beginning by establishing themes and ideas that structure the Divine Comedy before moving into questions and exercises meant to strengthen intuition and imagination.

claims.claim: Jiang frames his lecture as only one interpretation and warns that reading the Divine Comedy in English introduces interpretive problems because the class does not know Italian.
claims.temporal_scope: Jiang methodological claim stated on 2026-06-15 about the limits of this class's translation-based reading.

claims.claim: Jiang says the Divine Comedy is an act of divine inspiration and that reading it aloud in Tuscan lets the reader channel Dante himself.
claims.temporal_scope: Jiang interpretive and spiritual claim stated on 2026-06-15.

claims.claim: Jiang says he treats the Divine Comedy as perfection, so if a passage seems confusing the failure lies in the reader's intuition and imagination rather than in Dante's words.
claims.temporal_scope: Jiang hermeneutic rule stated on 2026-06-15 for this course.

claims.claim: Jiang interprets Dante as rejecting mere obedience to priestly authority and says real understanding requires open debate in which students are allowed to make errors.
claims.temporal_scope: Jiang pedagogical and historical interpretation stated on 2026-06-15.

claims.claim: Jiang treats Dante's image of heaven as a body as a prompt to test how different metaphors alter what the universe seems to be.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang says only the Tuscan read aloud lets you experience the poem by channeling Dante himself.
signature_moments.source_phrase: you will be channeling dante himself
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It captures the packet's most charged claim about language, voice, and why translation cannot fully replace the original performance.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang treats every apparent confusion in the poem as a failure of the reader rather than a flaw in Dante.
signature_moments.source_phrase: it's not his fault it's our fault
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's governing classroom stance and sets the severity of Jiang's hermeneutic method.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang turns Dante into a defense of debate against simple obedience to church authority.
signature_moments.source_phrase: you have to engage in open debate
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It links Jiang's reading of the poem directly to his own teaching method and to a larger anti-passive model of understanding.

signature_moments.moment: The universe-as-body line becomes a live exercise in how metaphors generate different worlds.
signature_moments.source_phrase: the metaphor that's being used is body
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It launches the metaphor workshop that shapes the next packets and makes interpretation itself the object of study.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's claim that Dante wrote the Divine Comedy by channeling God and the universe rather than merely composing an ordinary text.
Jiang's working assumption that every word and idea in the Divine Comedy is perfect, so interpretive failure belongs to the reader.
The practice Jiang says is necessary for real understanding, opposed to passive obedience to institutional authority.
The initial metaphor for the universe that Jiang uses to open a comparison of alternative cosmological images.

chronology_notes.note: This packet marks the afternoon restart of the June 15 livestream and resets the course method before the extended universe-metaphor discussion begins.
